title: They Waited for Marriage… So Why Does It Hurt Now?
paragraphs:
They Waited for Marriage… So Why Does It Hurt Now?
The Quiet Crisis of Christian Intimacy—and the Gospel That Heals What No One Talks About
No one warned them that the silence would follow them into the bedroom.

They were faithful. They resisted. They prayed. They said no when everything in them wanted to say yes. They honored God in the dark when nobody was watching. They built their love on Scripture, not on impulse.
And then… the wedding came.
The vows were spoken. The covenant sealed. The ring slipped onto trembling fingers. The room erupted with celebration. Heaven smiled.
And that night—the night they were told would finally be free, holy, beautiful, unrestrained—it felt… confusing.
Awkward.
Heavy.
Sometimes even painful.
They didn’t say it out loud. Not to friends. Not to church. Not even to each other at first.
But something wasn’t right.
And now they’re lying side by side in the dark, wondering…
“Why does this feel harder than it’s supposed to?”
This is the quiet crisis so many Christian couples carry behind closed doors.
Because we taught them how to say no.
But we never taught them how to say yes.
And the truth is… Scripture never shamed intimacy. We did.

From the beginning, God did not whisper sexuality into existence—He declared it. In the Hebrew, Genesis 2:24 says:
“וְדָבַק בְּאִשְׁתּוֹ” (ve’davaq b’ishto)—“and he shall cling, cleave, be joined to his wife.”
That word davaq is not passive. It is fierce attachment. It is pursuit. It is intimacy that binds soul and body together.
And then comes the line that most churches read quickly and never sit in long enough:

“וַיִּהְיוּ שְׁנֵיהֶם עֲרוּמִּים… וְלֹא יִתְבֹּשָׁשׁוּ”
“They were both naked… and not ashamed.” (Genesis 2:25)
No shame.
No hiding.
No performance.
No fear.
Just presence.
Just union.
Just God in the middle of it.
But somewhere along the way, many believers didn’t just flee sin…
They learned to fear their own bodies.
They learned that desire was dangerous.
That arousal was suspicious.
That sexuality was something to suppress, manage, control, survive.
So they built years—sometimes decades—of internal resistance.
And then one day, they stood at an altar and expected that switch to flip instantly.
But trauma doesn’t disappear with a wedding ring.
Conditioning doesn’t dissolve with vows.
Fear doesn’t vanish just because something became “allowed.”
So now intimacy feels like pressure instead of freedom.
Like obligation instead of connection.
Like performance instead of presence.
And nobody talks about it.
Because they’re supposed to be the “godly couple.”
But listen carefully… because this is where everything begins to change.
God never designed sex as a test of performance.
He designed it as a language of covenant.

In the Greek, 1 Corinthians 7:3 says:
“ὁ ἀνὴρ τῇ γυναικὶ τὴν ὀφειλὴν ἀποδιδότω” (ho anēr tē gynaiki tēn opheilēn apodidotō)
“The husband should give to his wife her due…”
But this is not a cold transaction.
It is mutual giving.
Mutual surrender.
Mutual honoring.
The passage continues by saying their bodies belong to each other—not as ownership, but as entrusted care.
And here’s what many miss…
Intimacy is not just physical access.
It is emotional safety.
It is spiritual vulnerability.
It is the removal of masks.
And if shame is still present, intimacy will struggle—no matter how “biblical” the marriage looks from the outside.
Some couples are fighting battles they don’t even realize have names.
Purity culture wounds.
Past sexual trauma.
Comparison.
Unrealistic expectations.
Pornography history.
Silence.
Fear of rejection.
Fear of failure.
And underneath it all… a quiet question:
“Am I enough?”
But the Gospel doesn’t ignore this.
It enters it.
Jesus never flinches at broken places.
He moves toward them.

The same Christ who restored Peter after denial…
who defended the woman caught in adultery…
who touched the untouchable…
is not uncomfortable with your marriage bed.
He is not distant from your struggle.
He is not ashamed of your questions.
Because redemption does not stop at salvation.
It flows into every hidden corner of your life—including your intimacy.
Song of Songs was never meant to be skipped.
It was meant to be felt.

“דּוֹדִי לִי וַאֲנִי לוֹ” (dodi li va’ani lo)
“My beloved is mine, and I am his.” (Song of Songs 2:16)
This is not lust.
This is covenant desire—redeemed, pure, alive.
And if your marriage feels distant right now…
You are not broken beyond repair.
You are not disqualified.
You are not alone.
Healing often begins with something simple but terrifying:
Honesty.
Real conversations.
Slow rebuilding.
Unlearning shame.
Inviting God into the space instead of leaving Him outside the door.
Because intimacy was never meant to be hidden from Him.
It was designed in His presence.
So if this exposed something you’ve been silently carrying…
Let that be your first step out of isolation.
And if you’re still fighting to believe your marriage can be restored…
Because that matters more than perfection ever will.
And if you want to grow deeper—not just in marriage, but in Christ Himself—stay close.
Because supporting this mission isn’t about money…
It’s about multiplying truth.
It’s about helping more marriages heal.
It’s about bringing light into places the church has been too quiet about.
The Gospel was never meant to stay comfortable.
It was meant to restore what shame tried to bury.
And maybe… just maybe…
your story isn’t falling apart.
Maybe Jesus is rewriting it—slowly, intimately, beautifully.
And one day you’ll look back at this struggle…
and realize it was the place grace found you both.
